newsitem.title: UK: Carlton's Green sets out case for DTT.
newsitem.headline: Carlton's Green sets out case for DTT.

text.p: Carlton Communications Plc chairman Michael Green set out the case for digital terrestrial television (DTT) on Friday, arguing that it would be "the television of the future".

"You don't need a cable. You don't need a dish. With one simple set top box that plugs into your existing aerial socket, you can receive 30 television channels," Green said, spelling out the appeal of DTT to viewers.
"Everything you enjoy watching today will remain free, but you'll get better pictures and much better sound," he added in a speech to the FT New Media and Broadcasting conference.
Green is chairman of the British Digital Broadcasting consortium, which is bidding for three DTT licences, capable of carrying an initial 15 channels.
British Digital Broadcasting unites Carlton, fellow ITV major Granada Group Plc and pay television operator British Sky Broadcasting Plc.
It faces competition for the DTT licences from DTN, owned by Nasdaq-listed cable company International CableTel.
The Independent Television Commission (ITC) is expected to announce its decision on the licences this spring and the DTT services will go on air in mid-1998.

Green said that extra choice would enhance the quality of British television, predicted the continued strength of free-to-air, advertiser supported TV and said that DTT would promote a more competitive pay TV market in the UK.
He noted that both the BBC and ITV were planning new free digital services as well as "simulcasting" existing programmes in the new format.
British Digital Broadcasting is planning to supply 12 subscription channels in its basic package, including new BBC pay channels. Green said these would cost little more than a daily newspaper.
Viewers who pay a higher rate will also receive up to three premium channels showing movies and sport.
"That's the strength of our digital terrestrial package. It brings together the best British producers with top sport and the most popular movies," he said.
"If DTT can be launched successfully, it will boost competition in pay television and provide an environment in which free-to-air televison can thrive," said Green.
"At a stroke, new companies - like Carlton - will have access to pay television markets," he added.
